rv.q: This standalone show showcases UK dance talent, but features a narrative that perhaps needs greater pace to match the kinetic energy of the music and dance.

But the thing with such a wide-ranging cast, who all specialise in different styles, is that the dance ends up being somewhere in the middle: everyone can do it but it doesn’t play to anyone’s strengths.
This is an innovative and daring experiment in bringing together dancers of different ages, trained in varied styles around the world.

That's what makes this reinterpretation of it, through an electronic remix by DJ Walde and vibrant new dance production directed by Tinuke Craig and choreographed by Alexzandra Sarmiento, such a distinct pleasure.
The result is a visually appealing production with many good ideas, some of which work better than others.

A LIFE IN FOUR SEASONS isn't necessarily going to set the dance world on fire and there was a notable lack of choreographic variety and wow factor, but as evenings and settings go, it was a thoroughly charming affair.

I failed to see, in the end, why the distinction was made between them – some of the movements, taken together, were something of a dance feast, but I didn’t think there was enough dramatic tension between the different body parts.
This is a short programme, its length dictated by the original music, but it is one that contains worlds.
Yet the production stops short of establishing clear individual traits or meaningful relationships between the three protagonists.
I found A Life in Four Seasons entertaining enough, though I felt that there wasn't sufficient variety in the movement between seasons.
Despite its imaginative concept and talented cast, A Life in Four Seasons never quite develops the emotional depth it seems to be reaching for.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this Vivaldi remix dance piece, praising its intergenerational casting and vibrant choreography but finding the emotional storytelling underpowered. The techno-classical fusion delights some while leaving others cold.
